text.title: langchain-rag-pipeline Core Rules
text.summary: Rules for building LangChain RAG pipelines: loaders, splitters, embeddings, retrievers, and the LCEL prompt shape.

rule.statement: Use RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with chunk_overlap ≈ 10% of chunk_size. Zero overlap splits relevant passages across chunks.
rule.rationale: Boundary-cut sentences cause recall@k drops on queries whose answer straddles the chunk boundary.

rule.statement: Hash document bodies for embedding-cache lookup; skip re-embedding when content_hash matches. Never key by file path alone.
rule.rationale: Re-indexing the same corpus under new paths doubled embedding cost in one prod incident; content_hash dedup is mandatory.

rule.statement: In the prompt template, put retrieved context FIRST, then the question, then explicit instruction to use only the context above.
rule.rationale: Models attend to recent tokens; context-first + instruction-after produces fewer answers that ignore the retrieval.

rule.statement: Default retriever_k = 4-6. Higher k floods the prompt; add a cross-encoder reranker if you must overfetch.
rule.rationale: Accuracy plateaus near k=5 for most corpora; bigger k adds tokens without lift.

rule.statement: Bind the LCEL chain as parallel retrieval + passthrough then prompt then llm then parser. Never serialize retrieval before passthrough.
rule.rationale: RunnableParallel composition is the only shape that retrieves and forwards the question concurrently.

rule.statement: Pick the embedding model from the same provider as the LLM where possible (e.g., OpenAI text-embedding-3 with GPT-4). Cross-provider drift is a real source of retrieval misses.
rule.rationale: Same-provider embeddings tend to align better with the model's internal representations.

rule.statement: For corpora over 1M tokens, pick a hosted vectorstore (Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector) over an in-memory Chroma. In-memory dies on restart and won't share across replicas.
rule.rationale: In-memory stores cannot survive horizontal scaling; production needs durability and shared state.

rule.statement: Hold out 20% of any labeled question set as a sealed eval used only in CI; never read it during dev.
rule.rationale: Leakage of the eval set into prompts inflates scores; sealing is the only defense.

rule.statement: When the profile is valid, the corpus is high-tier (at or above 1M tokens) and documents are long (avg_doc_chars above 10× chunk_size, so one chunk cannot stand for its document), the decision-record MUST choose the advanced variant: a hosted vectorstore per r7, hierarchical retrieval that indexes small child chunks but returns their parent section (LangChain's ParentDocumentRetriever or an equivalent two-level scheme), overfetch of up to 20 candidates passed through a cross-encoder reranker and cut to the 4-6 that reach the prompt, and document-level metadata (title, section, source) stored on every chunk. The reranker's latency is added to the retrieval p95 and MUST still fit latency_budget_ms, otherwise the record falls back to r-default-high and says so in rejected alternatives; audit.rule_refs cites r4 and r7.

rationale.source: LangChain documentation (ParentDocumentRetriever, contextual compression and rerankers); rules r4 and r7 of this methodology

rule.rationale: In long documents the chunk that matches the query is rarely the chunk that answers it — the answer sits in the surrounding section — and plain top-k returns five near-duplicate fragments of one document. Two-level retrieval restores the context, and the reranker is the sanctioned way to overfetch under r4; LangChain's ParentDocumentRetriever documentation describes exactly this small-to-embed, large-to-return pattern.

rule.statement: When the profile is valid, the corpus is high-tier (doc_count × avg_doc_chars / 4 at or above 1M tokens) and documents are ordinary length (avg_doc_chars at most 10× the chosen chunk_size), the decision-record MUST choose the high-tier default: a hosted or server-side vectorstore (pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate) per r7, incremental indexing keyed by content_hash so a re-run embeds only changed documents, batched embedding calls with rate-limit retry, retriever_k in the 4-6 band with a metadata filter when query_pattern names a document subset, and no reranker. Measured retrieval latency at p95 is recorded in the record against latency_budget_ms; audit.rule_refs cites r2, r4 and r7.

rationale.source: LangChain documentation (vectorstore integrations, indexing API); rules r2, r4 and r7 of this methodology

rule.rationale: Past a million tokens the index outlives any single process and a full re-embed costs real money, so durability and incremental indexing stop being optional (r7, r2). Ordinary-length documents are represented well by a handful of chunks, which is why plain top-k with a filter still answers and a reranker's extra hop would spend latency budget on a problem the corpus does not have.

rule.statement: When the profile is valid and the corpus is low-tier — doc_count × avg_doc_chars / 4 under 1M tokens (the r7 line) — the decision-record MUST choose the cheap default: a disk-persisted local vectorstore (Chroma with a persist directory, not in-memory), RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with chunk_size 500-1000 characters and 10% overlap, retriever_k=4, no reranker, and one embedding model from the LLM's provider. The index is built in a single pass with the content_hash cache from r2 enabled, and audit.rule_refs cites r1, r2 and r4. Adding a hosted store, a reranker or a second embedding model on this tier requires a rejected-alternatives entry explaining which driver forced it.

rationale.source: LangChain documentation (Chroma vectorstore, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter); rules r2, r4 and r7 of this methodology

rule.rationale: Below a million tokens the whole index embeds for cents and fits one process, so every added component is latency and operational surface without recall to show for it; the accuracy plateau near k=5 in r4 holds most clearly on small corpora. LangChain's Chroma integration persists to a directory in one argument, which removes the only real failure of the local tier — losing the index on restart.
